title: Tracy Does Conan

jokes.text: Why is there hair everywhere? Did you shave in the kitchen? / The water in here is softer.
jokes.setup: Liz discovers hair all over the kitchen and asks if Dennis shaved there.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's entirely sincere, logical-to-him justification — 'The water in here is softer' — reveals he genuinely thinks this is reasonable.
jokes.explanation: A tight cold-open joke that efficiently establishes Dennis as a delusional, oblivious man-child. The punchline is specific enough to feel earned — 'softer water' sounds like something a real idiot would believe — and lands well on first viewing.

jokes.text: Look at this ski-jumping idiot, Bode Miller. What kind of a fruity name is Bode?
jokes.setup: Dennis is watching the Olympics on TV.
jokes.punchline: His critique of Bode Miller zeroes in on the name rather than anything athletic — revealing his misplaced priorities and general idiocy.
jokes.explanation: A competent character joke — Dennis's dumb macho posturing against a famous athlete — but fairly generic. The name-critique angle is mildly funny but not especially inventive.

jokes.text: That cereal has the Olympics on it? It must be eight months old.
jokes.setup: Dennis notices Olympic branding on a cereal box in the kitchen.
jokes.punchline: Rather than any sentimental or athletic observation, he immediately clocks the cereal's age via the promotional tie-in — a hilariously mundane and specific deduction.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. The joke works because it's an accurate and specific observation delivered with complete conviction — a real piece of observational logic hiding in a mundane domestic scene. It's the kind of small, smart joke 30 Rock excels at.

jokes.text: When you and me have kids, we're gonna give them good names, like Shannon or Rick. / When we what?
jokes.setup: Dennis casually mentions 'when you and me have kids' as though this is an established plan.
jokes.punchline: Liz's stunned 'When we what?' reveals this is entirely in Dennis's head — the audience and Liz are equally blindsided by his presumption.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured misdirection. Dennis slips the bombshell into a mundane name-preference sentence, and Liz's minimal reaction ('When we what?') is perfectly calibrated. The choice of 'Shannon or Rick' as 'good names' is also a tiny, effective character detail.

jokes.text: Look at this maze. It's so easy. You have to go in here, and out there.
jokes.setup: Dennis is doing a children's maze puzzle on a cereal box while proclaiming his mastery of it.
jokes.punchline: His complete self-satisfaction at solving an extremely simple children's puzzle underscores his arrested development.
jokes.explanation: A functional character joke. It works as an accumulation of Dennis details rather than a standalone brilliant joke. Part of a rapid-fire cold-open barrage establishing his stupidity.

jokes.text: Hmm, 35, single, no children. Three sexual partners in the last ten years. / I don't know, doll. Maybe it's time to settle.
jokes.setup: Liz is getting a check-up and announces she's breaking up with her boyfriend tonight — framing it as a positive step.
jokes.punchline: The doctor reads her stats back like a grim tally and advises her to 'settle' — completely undermining her optimism with cold statistical pessimism.
jokes.explanation: A sharp, dark joke. The doctor weaponizes medical detachment to deliver a devastating social judgment. 'Three sexual partners in the last ten years' is a specific, cruel number and 'Maybe it's time to settle' is both advice and an insult. Strong structure, earns its cringe.

jokes.text: Chocolate chip, or butter crunch?
jokes.setup: The doctor has just delivered a devastating verdict on Liz's romantic life. The scene should pivot to something professional.
jokes.punchline: Instead, the doctor casually offers cookie options — completely breaking clinical decorum and suggesting this is just a normal part of his bedside manner.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed non-sequitur. The extreme economy — just five words — and the complete tonal whiplash after the devastating 'settle' line make this land. The absurdity of a doctor offering cookie flavors is perfectly underplayed.

jokes.text: The Rural Juror — the title is so difficult to say that Pete literally cannot complete it, calling it 'The Rur-- That one.'
jokes.setup: Pete tries to reference Jenna's movie 'The Rural Juror' to comfort her.
jokes.punchline: The title is phonetically nearly impossible to say, so Pete trails off into 'The Rur-- That one' — the first instance of what becomes the episode's running gag.
jokes.explanation: One of 30 Rock's great recurring bits. The joke is genuinely brilliant: it's meta (a bad title that is itself almost unpronounceably bad), it generates automatic callbacks, and 'The Rur-- That one' is an immediately quotable piece of physical/verbal comedy. Sets up an entire episode-long running gag with one title.

jokes.text: 'Rural Juror, apple three, take one. Mark! A terrible title. Action!'
jokes.setup: We see a clip from the filming of 'The Rural Juror.'
jokes.punchline: Even the director on set announces mid-slate 'A terrible title' before calling action — the joke is that everyone involved knew it was bad.
jokes.explanation: Escalates the Rural Juror gag beautifully. The director editorializing mid-clapperboard is absurd and specific. The joke commits to the bit — everyone in this fictional universe agrees it's a terrible title.

jokes.text: Jenna is paged to the set for 'Rodney Stink Confirmed Bachelor' — another hilariously bad fictional show title.
jokes.setup: A PA announcement calls Jenna to set.
jokes.punchline: The show she's being called to is 'Rodney Stink Confirmed Bachelor' — a title so aggressively bad it's funny on its own.
jokes.explanation: A quick background gag in 30 Rock's tradition of absurdly-named fake shows. 'Rodney Stink Confirmed Bachelor' is committed enough to the bit to earn a genuine laugh. Economy is the strength here.

jokes.text: "The Rural Juror" opens in selected theaters December 18th. / Does Jack Donaghy even know I'm in The Rural Juror?
jokes.setup: An official-sounding announcement of the film's release, followed by Jenna's concern about whether Jack knows.
jokes.punchline: Both lines are funny — the first for the dry delivery of 'selected theaters' (damning with faint praise), and Jenna's line for attempting to say the full title straight, now a comedic landmine every time.
jokes.explanation: 'Selected theaters' is a quietly brutal joke about the film's commercial prospects. Jenna saying the title normally while everyone else can't is a good structural contrast in the running gag.

jokes.text: I will tell him that you are in a feature film called The Rrr Jrr.
jokes.setup: Liz promises to advocate for Jenna to Jack by mentioning her film.
jokes.punchline: Liz reduces the phonetically impossible title to pure consonant soup: 'The Rrr Jrr' — showing even she can't say it.
jokes.explanation: The best iteration of the Rural Juror gag so far. 'The Rrr Jrr' is a genuine comedic invention — reducing a bad title to pure growl-sounds. Extremely quotable and perfectly economical.

jokes.text: What the hell's her movie called? / I don't know. She's been talking about it for a year. / I can't ask her now.
jokes.setup: Liz and Pete discuss Jenna's movie, which Jenna mentions constantly.
jokes.punchline: Neither of them can recall the title despite her constant promotion — and it's been a full year.
jokes.explanation: Solid structural callback that reinforces why the title joke works — it's not that people don't care, it's that the title is literally unmemorable due to phonetics. 'I can't ask her now' is a real piece of social awkwardness comedy.

jokes.text: Tracy's previous Conan appearance flashback: 'You seem like you have a nice chemistry...' / 'I am a stabbing robot. I will stab you.'
jokes.setup: Characters mention Tracy's disastrous previous Conan appearance. We cut to the clip.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response to Conan's warm banter is to declare himself a stabbing robot and threaten to stab him — delivered with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'I am a stabbing robot. I will stab you.' is instantly iconic — specific, absurd, completely in character, and utterly committed. The contrast with Conan's gentle 'nice chemistry' remark is perfect. This is a genuine 8.5+ joke: it's quotable, character-specific, and structurally airtight. The callback potential (real Conan, real late night) adds a layer of meta-comedy.

jokes.text: Jack complimenting Liz on the Stone Phillips wig: 'I know you're wearing that as a joke, but it makes you look younger, and more confident, and I think you should consider it.'
jokes.setup: Liz is wearing the ridiculous Stone Phillips wig as a joke when Jack sees her.
jokes.punchline: Jack, completely earnestly, tells her it makes her look younger and more confident — his fashion authority is so strong he sees real potential in a comedy wig.
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke. Jack's unironic sincerity about a joke wig perfectly illustrates his patrician confidence — he's so assured in his own taste that he can find merit where none is intended. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Jack bumped Jenna because she 'does commercials for ShopRite' — Liz defends her: 'Jenna doesn't do those commercials anymore. She got fired.'
jokes.setup: Liz defends Jenna against Jack's dismissal of her as a ShopRite commercial actress.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defense — 'she doesn't do those anymore, she got fired' — makes things worse, not better. It's meant to be exculpatory but only underscores Jenna's lack of prestige.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured ironic joke. The punchline lands because Liz intends it as vindication but the audience immediately clocks that being fired from ShopRite commercials is not an improvement. Great economy and earned execution.

jokes.text: Jack: 'That's why my job is way better than yours. /Way better.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains that Liz always has to clean up his messes afterward.
jokes.punchline: He ends with 'That's why my job is way better than yours. /Way better.' — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is a logical conclusion to a reasonable argument.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Jack's unapologetic elitism is perfectly voiced — but the joke is fairly predictable given the setup. The '/Way better.' emphasis is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Conan: 'I like to surround myself with people that don't try to stab me.'
jokes.setup: Jack pitches Tracy appearing on Conan's show again.
jokes.punchline: Conan, playing himself, delivers a perfectly dry objection based on Tracy literally trying to stab him previously.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback. The joke works because Conan is playing himself and his objection is completely reasonable — the absurdity is that 'don't stab me' is a legitimate prerequisite for being a guest. The understatement of framing it as a general preference is well done.

jokes.text: Conan: 'That's what they said about Hasselhoff, then he tried to make out with me during a commercial break.'
jokes.setup: Jack assures Conan that Tracy is 'under a doctor's care' now.
jokes.punchline: Conan counters with a specific, vivid anecdote about Hasselhoff making out with him — a completely unexpected and absurd specific detail delivered as casual complaint.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. The specificity of Hasselhoff making out with Conan during a commercial break is perfectly absurd, the celebrity name-drop has a genuine twist (it's not just a mention — it's a weird and specific accusation), and Conan delivers it as if it's a reasonable concern. The 'during a commercial break' detail elevates it from funny to hilarious. Comfortably in 8+ territory.

jokes.text: Jack: 'You do a live Christmas Eve special from Kabul every year until the war on terror is won.'
jokes.setup: Jack offers Conan a choice: 'the easy way or the hard way.'
jokes.punchline: The 'hard way' turns out to be an NBC programming punishment — Christmas Eve specials from Kabul indefinitely, tied to the unknowable end of the war on terror.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. It works on multiple levels: Jack's corporate power is absurdly large (he can program NBC as a personal threat), the specific punishment is brilliantly conceived (Christmas Eve + Kabul + 'until the war on terror is won' = indefinite hell), and it's a perfect Jack character joke — his authority is so vast it becomes surreal. Highly quotable. Justifies 8.4 craft.

jokes.text: Conan: 'Tell Tracy I'll see him tonight. You, black Irish bastard.' / Jack: 'Back at you, man.'
jokes.setup: After Jack's threat, Conan concedes and gives his parting shot.
jokes.punchline: The exchange — 'black Irish bastard' / 'back at you' — plays as genuine masculine warmth/respect between two powerful men, suggesting this is their normal register.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke about the way alpha males communicate. The specificity of 'black Irish' and Jack's easy 'back at you' implies this is a relationship with its own shorthand. Funny and economical.

jokes.text: Tracy's pitch: 'Me and my wife like to play rape. She goes in the bathroom and does her hair. Then I put on a ski mask...' / 'Okay, not that.'
jokes.setup: The writers ask Tracy to share anecdotes from his personal life that could be punched up for Conan.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's first offering is a 'role play' scenario that escalates into something deeply alarming — Liz cuts him off after 'ski mask.'
jokes.explanation: A strong character joke — only Tracy would pitch this on a morning writers' session. The escalation structure (innocent start → ski mask) is well-paced, and Liz's 'Okay, not that' is perfectly calibrated. The joke relies on Tracy's specific brand of oblivious wildness.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'I like to walk around my house naked, to remind my oldest son who's still got the biggest ding dong.'
jokes.setup: Writers ask for stories about Tracy being a dad, since 'people eat that garbage up.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy's fatherhood anecdote is about competitive nudity and genital dominance hierarchy within his family.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The setup — cute dad stories — is expertly misdirected into something completely unhinged. 'Who's still got the biggest ding dong' is specific, confident, and utterly Tracy. It's also genuinely surprising even on rewatch because the build is so efficient. High quotability, strong character integration. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'I can tell the story of how I met Sharon Stone. I was pooping in the ladies' room at the Ivy...'
jokes.setup: Tracy offers another anecdote option — meeting a celebrity, which sounds promising.
jokes.punchline: He was 'pooping in the ladies' room at the Ivy' — the combination of wrong bathroom + wrong activity + celebrity restaurant + Sharon Stone is a perfect absurdist pile-up.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist character joke. The three-way specificity (ladies' room, pooping, The Ivy) in a single clause is economical and surprising. The 'No.' from Liz as the entire response is perfect.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'My hair hurts.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is in the middle of a prep session for the show.
jokes.punchline: Tracy announces 'My hair hurts' — a medically nonsensical complaint delivered as if it's totally normal.
jokes.explanation: Three words. 'My hair hurts' is a perfect Tracy non-sequitur — impossible, delivered straight, and entirely consistent with someone who's experiencing a medication reaction. Extreme economy. The joke's brevity is its greatest asset.

jokes.text: Tracy insisting the phone is ringing when there is no phone ringing: 'Is anybody gonna answer the phone? The phone! It's ringing! Ring! Ring!'
jokes.setup: Tracy appears to be hallucinating.
jokes.punchline: He becomes increasingly agitated about a completely silent room, escalating to literally saying 'Ring! Ring!' himself — the medication reaction manifesting as comic psychosis.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from confused question to shouting 'Ring! Ring!' himself is well-structured absurdism. Tracy performing the sound effect he believes he's hearing is a specific, committed comedic choice.

jokes.text: Liz's pitch: 'I haven't seen this many white people in tuxedoes since the Titanic.'
jokes.setup: Liz is asked to write an opening quip for a $1,000-a-plate fundraiser.
jokes.punchline: Her joke invokes mass death and the Titanic as a punchline about wealthy white people.
jokes.explanation: A reasonably sharp joke — invoking the Titanic as a rich-white-people death event is pointed — but Jack's dismissal of it as 'open mike night at the Bryn Mawr student union' is funnier than the joke itself, which is the actual joke.

jokes.text: Jack's dismissal: 'Lemon, this is not open mike night at the Bryn Mawr student union.'
jokes.setup: Liz offers her Titanic joke as a quality quip.
jokes.punchline: Jack's specific cultural demolition — 'open mike night at the Bryn Mawr student union' — is precisely calibrated to insult both the quality and the demographic of the joke.
jokes.explanation: Strong Jack joke. 'Bryn Mawr student union' is a perfectly specific insult — it implies Liz's comedy is earnest, liberal-arts-feminism-flavored, and completely inappropriate for a corporate gala. The specificity elevates it above a generic dismissal.

jokes.text: Jack's pitch: 'Jack Welch has such unparalleled management skills, they named Welch's grape juice after him. Because he squeezes the sweetest juice out of his workers' mind grapes.'
jokes.setup: Jack presents his own alternative quip — which he clearly thinks is excellent.
jokes.punchline: The joke is deeply nonsensical — Welch's grape juice is not named after Jack Welch, the metaphor is garbled, and 'mind grapes' is an invented phrase that means nothing — but Jack is completely proud of it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great jokes and a genuine 30 Rock classic. 'Mind grapes' is a perfect absurdist invention — it sounds corporate-motivational but means absolutely nothing. The joke is also perfectly Jack: he's confident, wrong, and completely unaware of how bad the joke is. Liz's 'That doesn't even make sense' and Jack's 'No, it doesn't, does it? I wrote it down in the middle of the night' is the perfect button. High quotability — 'mind grapes' entered the show's vocabulary.

jokes.text: Liz: 'That doesn't even make sense.' Jack: 'No, it doesn't, does it? I wrote it down in the middle of the night.'
jokes.setup: Jack presents 'mind grapes' as if it's quality material.
jokes.punchline: Jack's cheerful admission that it doesn't make sense, explained by 'I wrote it down in the middle of the night' — the confession is so casual and self-aware it loops back to being funny.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the mind grapes joke. Jack's complete lack of embarrassment about being caught — 'No, it doesn't, does it?' — is the ideal character response. It's not ignorance, it's a strange form of confident self-awareness that only Jack could pull off. The economy is excellent: one sentence explains everything about the kind of executive who trusts his 3am thoughts.

jokes.text: Jack: 'What else is on my mind grapes?'
jokes.setup: Jack continues thinking out loud after the mind grapes conversation.
jokes.punchline: He has immediately adopted 'mind grapes' as his own vocabulary — using it naturally as if it's a real phrase — despite just admitting it doesn't make sense.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback. Jack using 'mind grapes' in casual conversation immediately after admitting it doesn't make sense is perfect character comedy — he likes how it sounds and that's enough for him. The self-referential quality (he coined a nonsense term and now uses it) is deeply funny. One of the episode's best moments for Jack's characterization.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'I could talk about how the moon is a spy satellite put there by Oprah and Minister Farrakhan. And not the minister Farrakhan you're thinking of.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is pitching Conan anecdotes.
jokes.punchline: The conspiracy theory is already wildly absurd (Oprah + Farrakhan + moon spy satellite), but 'and not the minister Farrakhan you're thinking of' implies there's a different, equally famous Minister Farrakhan — deepening the nonsense.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The two-sentence structure is masterful: the first sentence is a great absurdist conspiracy theory, and the second sentence adds a layer of impossibility on top of it ('not the one you're thinking of' implies there's an alternate Farrakhan). This is 30 Rock at its densest and most inventive. High quotability, perfect character integration, brilliant economy. Justifies 8.5.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Who's that dude? / Uh, what dude? / The blue dude. Tell him to stop staring at me.'
jokes.setup: Tracy appears to be hallucinating.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is seeing a 'blue dude' that nobody else can see — his first hallucination, delivered with complete sincerity and an almost polite request to stop staring.
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the blue man running gag. The politeness of 'tell him to stop staring at me' while hallucinating is a nice character touch. This is more of a running gag launcher than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Meep.
jokes.setup: Tracy has been ranting at the Blue Man, demanding he stop staring.
jokes.punchline: The Blue Man's only response is 'Meep.' — a tiny, non-threatening vocalization from an entity Tracy is terrified of, which deflates the tension entirely.
jokes.explanation: A single syllable that lands hard. 'Meep' is the perfect comedic response — it acknowledges the Blue Man is real and sentient, but his communication is so minimal and harmless that it makes Tracy's terror even more absurd. Maximum economy (one word, technically), excellent structure as a punchline to the blue man setup. The word 'Meep' is inherently funny. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Tracy is found in a prop closet, apparently on the phone — 'Yes. I am having problems with my cable television. Yes, I will hold.'
jokes.setup: Everyone searches for Tracy after his breakdown.
jokes.punchline: He's been found having a completely normal cable TV complaint call — the mundane domesticity of the call is the joke given the level of crisis around him.
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist joke. Amid a crisis, Tracy is on hold with a cable company — the normality is the joke. The detail of 'I will hold' is the perfect button: he's being patient and cooperative about cable while everyone panics.

jokes.text: Tracy interrupts his crisis moment to take another call: 'Excuse me, I have another call. Hi, mom. I am doing fine.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is in the middle of a meltdown/cable call.
jokes.punchline: He clicks over to talk to his mother with complete normalcy — 'I am doing fine' — while everything around him is chaos.
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective absurdist beat. Tracy's 'I am doing fine' to his mom, delivered with complete sincerity while mid-hallucination, is perfectly timed. The formality of 'I am doing fine' (not 'I'm fine') adds a nice touch.

jokes.text: Frank eats Liz's blood cookie — 'Oh, that's not good. Frank, that was my blood cookie.'
jokes.setup: Liz had taken a cookie for giving blood. Frank eats it.
jokes.punchline: 'Blood cookie' is a hilariously specific compound noun — calling it 'my blood cookie' implies an understood category of food that does not actually exist.
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny background joke. 'Blood cookie' is a great piece of 30 Rock's specific-compound-noun comedy. The 'Ew, what?' reaction from someone off-screen is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Pete wearing the Stone Phillips wig walks into the hall; Jack double-takes and says 'Hey, Jack Attack. Sorry, I should have kept that one in the old brain box.'
jokes.setup: Pete is wearing the hairpiece. Jack sees him from behind and mistakes him briefly for someone attractive/powerful.
jokes.punchline: Jack catches himself calling Pete 'Jack Attack' (apparently his own nickname) and immediately regrets the overfamiliarity — 'I should have kept that one in the old brain box.'
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. 'The old brain box' is a Jack-specific piece of vocabulary — slightly pompous and slightly absurd. The fact that the wig is powerful enough to trick Jack for a split-second is the visual joke, and his immediate social retreat is the verbal punchline.

jokes.text: Jack to Pete: 'Did you know that men with full heads of hair on average earn 17% more than their bald counterparts? / I did not know that. / Perhaps it's because bald men are generally less informed than men with full heads of hair.'
jokes.setup: Jack is pushing Pete to wear the wig by citing a statistic.
jokes.punchline: Jack uses the statistic itself as evidence for the statistic — 'Perhaps it's because bald men are generally less informed' — meaning Pete's ignorance of the stat proves the stat.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best jokes. The logic is circular and completely airtight from Jack's perspective: he cites the statistic, Pete doesn't know it, Jack uses Pete's ignorance as proof of the statistic. It's a perfect piece of Jack's patrician pseudo-logic — confident, unfalsifiable, and slightly cruel. The structure is impeccable. Justifies 8.7.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Pull my hair. Right now, go ahead. Pull my hair.' / Pete pulls it. / Jack: 'I'm just kidding. It's real.'
jokes.setup: Jack invites Pete to pull his hair to prove it's real.
jokes.punchline: Pete does, hurting Jack slightly, and Jack says 'I'm just kidding. It's real.' — which means he invited the pull but also seems to have been testing something, and 'I'm just kidding' is a strange thing to say about a genuine demonstration.
jokes.explanation: A nicely structured physical comedy bit. 'I'm just kidding. It's real.' is a paradoxical statement — the 'just kidding' makes no sense after a genuine hair-pull demonstration — which is exactly the kind of non-sequitur payoff 30 Rock likes. Good economy.

jokes.text: Liz relays Jack's opinion: 'He doesn't love it that you did those commercials.' / Jenna: 'Well, you tell him that those commercials paid for my vacation home. So, unless he would like to buy me a condo in Clearwater, Florida...'
jokes.setup: Jenna learns Jack judges her for the ShopRite commercials.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's defense is that the commercials funded a vacation home — but specifying 'Clearwater, Florida' perfectly calibrates how unimpressive this is as a status symbol.
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke. 'Clearwater, Florida' is the punchline — it tells you everything about Jenna's actual status. Her defiant pride about a Florida condo is funny because it confirms Jack's dismissal.

jokes.text: Well, you tell him that those commercials paid for my vacation home. So, unless he would like to buy me a condo in Clearwater, Florida...
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jenna that Jack views the commercials as a mark against her.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's counter-argument is the vacation home, which she then undercuts by specifying it's a condo in Clearwater, Florida — an aspirational flex that reveals a humbling reality about her actual star power.
jokes.explanation: A good Jenna character joke. 'Vacation home' suggests wealth; 'condo in Clearwater, Florida' deflates it perfectly. Clearwater is funny because it's neither glamorous nor humble — it's exactly the level of achievement that is somehow both pathetic and defensible. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Tracy's full breakdown: 'I'm bugging out! I'm bugging out!' repeated while apparently bouncing around the room.
jokes.setup: Liz enters Tracy's dressing room to check on him.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is in full meltdown, repeatedly announcing 'I'm bugging out!' — the self-narration of a breakdown is its own comedy.
jokes.explanation: More physical comedy than conceptual joke — effective but not exceptional. The humor is in Tracy's self-awareness about bugging out while bugging out, but it's mainly a performance beat rather than a written joke.

jokes.text: Wow, Dr. Spaceman. I owe you an apology, Tray.
jokes.setup: Liz finds Tracy's medicine and sees 'Dr. Spaceman' is actually the doctor's name.
jokes.punchline: Liz had assumed it was a delusion; seeing the bottle confirms it's real. Her apology to Tracy — who is currently losing his mind — is a funny inversion of expected concern.
jokes.explanation: A nice beat — Liz's 'I owe you an apology' to a hallucinating man in crisis is funny because her priority is correcting her assumption about the name rather than helping him. Character-consistent and economical.

jokes.text: Dr. Spaceman: 'Medicine's not a science.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman explains the unpredictable drug interactions Tracy faces.
jokes.punchline: 'Medicine's not a science' — delivered as a casual observation by a licensed physician, as if this is a commonly understood fact.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Four words. 'Medicine's not a science.' is a perfectly constructed absurdist line: it's the exact opposite of what a doctor should believe, delivered with complete confidence and no self-awareness. It instantly defines Dr. Spaceman as a character, is endlessly quotable, and functions as one of 30 Rock's most celebrated recurring lines. This is the 9+ territory — comparable in economy and impact to the great anchor examples. It has become a cultural touchstone for the show.

jokes.text: Dr. Spaceman: 'And certainly not helped by my wildly experimental treatments. Boy, I'm being awfully open with you, miss.'
jokes.setup: Spaceman describes Tracy's condition.
jokes.punchline: His self-correction — 'Boy, I'm being awfully open with you, miss' — implies a sudden awareness that admitting to 'wildly experimental treatments' on a patient may not be professional.
jokes.explanation: An excellent follow-up joke. 'Wildly experimental treatments' is the first absurdity, but the button — 'Boy, I'm being awfully open with you' — adds a layer of social awkwardness that implies Spaceman knows he shouldn't be saying this but is saying it anyway. The 'miss' is a nice period-out-of-time touch. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dr. Spaceman's care instructions: 'Keep him away from bright lights, loud music and crowds.' — for a man about to appear on a late night talk show.
jokes.setup: Dr. Spaceman gives instructions for keeping Tracy stable.
jokes.punchline: The instructions — bright lights, loud music, crowds — are precisely a description of a live TV taping. The dramatic irony is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed dramatic irony joke. The three prohibitions (bright lights, loud music, crowds) are a perfect description of the very environment Tracy is being sent to. The audience connects the dots and the payoff is immediate. Clean structure.

jokes.text: Dr. Spaceman: 'Uh... do you need anything for yourself?'
jokes.setup: Liz asks where to pick up Tracy's prescription.
jokes.punchline: Spaceman casually offers to prescribe Liz something 'for herself' — implying he's the kind of doctor who just hands out pills to anyone who calls.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Spaceman character joke. The casual 'do you need anything for yourself?' implies he casually prescribes narcotics to anyone he speaks to. Economy is excellent — one question does all the work. Strong character integration: this joke could only be Dr. Spaceman.

jokes.text: When I first met Jack Welch, I thought he was such a great golfer, he made Bob Darnell look like Randy Barnes. / That's fine. Do that. / I don't know. Might be distasteful if Randy's widow's in the audience.
jokes.setup: Jack shares his latest Welch zinger attempt — a golf comparison.
jokes.punchline: Liz approves, Jack suddenly worries about 'Randy's widow' — implying Randy Barnes is dead, turning what seemed like an innocuous sports reference into a potential faux pas involving a widow.
jokes.explanation: A dark gag — casual mention of someone being dead, framed as a social etiquette concern. The comedy is Jack suddenly becoming concerned about decorum after everything else in this episode. Mildly funny but the Randy Darnell/Barnes references are obscure enough to limit impact.

jokes.text: Jack says Tracy's doctor Spaceman is 'an excellent physician. And a pretty good dentist.'
jokes.setup: Liz calls the doctor; Jack vouches for Dr. Spaceman.
jokes.punchline: 'And a pretty good dentist' — Spaceman is practicing multiple specialties, adding to his terrifying medical profile. The 'pretty good' qualifier is doing a lot of work.
jokes.explanation: A great Spaceman callback. 'Pretty good dentist' is the perfect qualifier — not a great dentist, just pretty good, and also he shouldn't be practicing dentistry at all given what we know. The joke deepens Spaceman's character with minimal words.

jokes.text: The rehearsal disaster — clearly something goes wrong (Liz: 'Is that rehearsal? Oh no--Oh!') followed by Jack's irritated 'No, this Tracy situation is really...' and Jack dismissing it: 'Are we still talking about that? Do I have to come in and run your show?'
jokes.setup: Liz is briefing Jack on the Tracy crisis while something is clearly going wrong off-camera in rehearsal.
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'Do I have to come in and run your show?' is a power move that reduces the entire crisis to an annoyance, delivered while apparently something is blowing up.
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat rather than a great joke. Jack's dismissiveness is well-characterized but the laugh depends mostly on performance and the off-camera chaos, which is harder to assess from transcript alone.

jokes.text: Pete walks in wearing the wig; Jack does a double-take: 'Who is this leader of men? What can I do for you, handsome?'
jokes.setup: Pete enters Jack's office still wearing the Stone Phillips wig.
jokes.punchline: Jack is so bowled over by the wig's effect that he treats Pete with the same respect he'd give an equal — 'What can I do for you, handsome?' — completely forgetting Pete is a subordinate.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the wig joke. Jack's 'leader of men' and treating Pete as an equal is a perfect expression of his thesis (hair = power) in action. The running gag is paying off well.

jokes.text: Jenna's theatrical resignation: 'After the way Jack treated me today, I can't work here anymore. I quit.' — then immediately staying when Liz says three vague compliments.
jokes.setup: Jenna announces she's quitting.
jokes.punchline: Liz deploys minimal flattery ('you're my muse, you're a modern-day Lucille Ball, you're prettier than Deborah Messing') and Jenna immediately caves — 'Well, if that's the way you feel, I'll stay.' The entire crisis evaporates in 20 seconds.
jokes.explanation: A good character comedy sequence. The speed of Jenna's collapse under the flimsiest praise is perfect — she demands to be told she's prettier than Deborah Messing and that's sufficient. Character-specific and well-paced.

jokes.text: Okay. Jenna don't quit. The show can't go on without you. You're my muse, you're a modern-day Lucille Ball. You're prettier than Deborah Messing.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to convince Jenna to stay by heaping on flattery.
jokes.punchline: The escalating praise plateaus at 'You're prettier than Deborah Messing' — a very specific, curiously modest compliment that reveals Liz is running low on ideas and/or doesn't actually believe any of this. 'Deborah Messing' instead of 'Debra Messing' is also a subtle joke.
jokes.explanation: Good structure — the flattery builds from legitimate ('muse,' 'Lucille Ball') to the hilariously deflated 'prettier than Deborah Messing.' The choice of Debra Messing as the comparative sets a very specific bar. The mispronunciation 'Deborah' is a nice throwaway detail suggesting Liz barely knows who she's invoking.

jokes.text: Dennis calls to ask Liz to buy Nickelback tickets via Ticketmaster — 'I would do it on your computer, but I'm downloading a game right now.'
jokes.setup: Dennis calls Liz during a crisis at work.
jokes.punchline: He needs her to buy Nickelback tickets because he's using his computer for a game download — a perfectly calibrated portrait of male uselessness circa 2006.
jokes.explanation: A strong Dennis joke. 'I'd do it on your computer but I'm downloading a game' is the perfect details-specific laziness joke — he can't multitask, but also Nickelback. The combination of band choice and reason elevates it.

jokes.text: Blue man! That blue dude keeps following me! Meek, eep.
jokes.setup: Tracy has another Blue Man encounter.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's 'Meek, eep' — apparently his attempt to communicate with or mimic the Blue Man — is a funny detail, as is his certainty the Blue Man is 'following' him.
jokes.explanation: A serviceable continuation of the Blue Man running gag. 'Meek, eep' as mimicry is a funny detail, but this iteration is less sharp than the original introduction. Running gags often diminish on third appearances without escalation.

jokes.text: Liz and Conan's awkward exchange: 'You still, um...' / 'How's your wife?' / 'Let's not do this, Elizabeth.' / 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: Conan begins a sentence he can't finish; Liz deflects to ask about his wife.
jokes.punchline: Conan's 'Let's not do this, Elizabeth' is delivered with a familiarity that implies a whole history — and Liz's immediate 'Okay' suggests she knows exactly what he means.
jokes.explanation: A very economical cringe/awkward comedy moment. The entire implied backstory between Liz and Conan is conveyed in five exchanges. 'Let's not do this, Elizabeth' — using her full name — is the perfect celebrity-ex-who's-moved-on energy. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Conan sees the cookies Tracy has licked: 'Whoa, he licked all of those.'
jokes.setup: A tray of cookies is visible — it becomes apparent Tracy has licked every single one.
jokes.punchline: Conan's perfectly dry 'Whoa, he licked all of those' delivers maximum information with minimum alarm — the reaction is so calm it becomes funnier.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag with great economy. 'He licked all of those' is funnier than any elaboration could be. The detail of 'all of those' (not just some) is the key specificity.

jokes.text: Liz addresses the Blue Man: 'Chewbacca, may I speak to Tracy, please?'
jokes.setup: Liz approaches the Blue Man, who is between her and Tracy.
jokes.punchline: She calls him 'Chewbacca' — either she's so frazzled she can't remember who he is, or she's deliberately using a sci-fi comparison for the blue-painted performer.
jokes.explanation: A great quick joke. 'Chewbacca' is a perfect wrong-celebrity name for a blue-painted performer — both are large, non-speaking, and vaguely alien. The politeness of 'may I speak to Tracy, please' while calling him the wrong name is charming.

jokes.text: Tracy, apparently hiding from 'Past Pete': 'Past Pete is here to kill Future Pete!'
jokes.setup: Liz asks how Tracy is doing.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has invented a time-travel delusion involving Pete — apparently Pete is now both a threat from the past and a future victim. 'It's going great' is Liz's response.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Past Pete is here to kill Future Pete!' is inventively absurd — Tracy has developed a coherent time-travel paranoid narrative focused inexplicably on Pete. The internal logic (past/future) is the brilliant touch. Liz's deadpan 'It's going great' is the perfect button. High quotability.

jokes.text: Kenneth whispering at the pharmacy: '[whispering] for Mr. Tracy Jordan' — apparently so embarrassed by the prescription that he whispers the patient name.
jokes.setup: Kenneth picks up Tracy's prescription.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth whispers Tracy's name at the pharmacy counter, implying either shame, star awe, or both.
jokes.explanation: A quick Kenneth character beat — his reverence for celebrities is funny here, as is his social awkwardness. More of a character texture moment than a fully developed joke.

jokes.text: Kenneth at a second pharmacy, on hold: 'Fine. I will try the other location. But frankly, LaDonica, you have not been real helpful.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is having trouble getting the prescription and calls a second location.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's polite but firm complaint — 'LaDonica, you have not been real helpful' — is delivered with the gentle dignity of someone who takes every interaction seriously, even a pharmacy hold.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Kenneth joke. The use of the pharmacist's name ('LaDonica'), the formal 'you have not been real helpful' (not 'weren't very helpful'), and the polite indignation are all exactly Kenneth. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Fine. I will try the other location. But frankly, LaDonica, you have not been real helpful.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been trying to pick up Tracy's prescription and apparently the pharmacy has been difficult.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's gentle but firm admonition to 'LaDonica' the pharmacist — 'you have not been real helpful' — is funny because of the contrast between the stakes (someone's health) and Kenneth's Southern-mannered understatement. His use of her name ('LaDonica') is a funny specific detail.
jokes.explanation: A great Kenneth joke. His devastating courtesy — holding someone accountable in the politest possible terms — is signature Kenneth. 'LaDonica' as a name is funny, and 'you have not been real helpful' as the harshest criticism he can muster is perfect character integration. The urgency of the situation vs. his tone is the joke.

jokes.text: Jack, still in a tuxedo, asks Liz for another zinger for the Jack Welch event — Liz asks when it is. 'February.' 'Why are you wearing a tux?' 'It's after 6:00. What am I, a farmer?'
jokes.setup: Liz notices Jack is in formal wear for what turns out to be an event months away.
jokes.punchline: 'It's after 6:00. What am I, a farmer?' — Jack's logic is that post-6pm tuxedo is simply correct dress, regardless of occasion. The 'farmer' comparison is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the all-time great Jack Donaghy jokes. 'It's after 6:00. What am I, a farmer?' is a perfect encapsulation of his character: patrician, unironic, operating by a social code so rigid it becomes absurd. 'What am I, a farmer?' is the ideal choice of comparison — rural, unprestigious, the opposite of Jack. This joke is comfortably in 8.5+ territory: it's highly quotable, character-defining, and has become one of 30 Rock's most referenced lines. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Liz's zinger attempt: 'Well, it's almost Thanksgiving, everybody. And I know what this crowd's giving thanks for. Estate tax reform.'
jokes.setup: Liz finally delivers an actual joke for Jack's speech — topical, pointed.
jokes.punchline: The estate tax reform punchline is genuinely sharp — it correctly identifies the financial interests of the $1,000-a-plate crowd and skewers them with specificity.
jokes.explanation: A legitimately good political joke. 'Estate tax reform' as the thing wealthy gala attendees are thankful for is specific and earned. Jack's response ('That is terrific. I really enjoyed that.') and then his worry about topicality is a good follow-up beat.

jokes.text: Jack: 'That is terrific. I really enjoyed that. But, do you think it's too topical? Damn, I wish this event were tonight.'
jokes.setup: Jack praises Liz's estate tax joke but is worried about shelf life.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the event is in February — when Liz asks 'When is it?' — makes Jack's worry about topicality retroactively absurd. He's worried about a joke's freshness for an event four months away.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured reveal. The punchline (event is in February) reframes Jack's concern as ridiculous while also setting up the tuxedo joke that follows. Good structural writing.

jokes.text: That is terrific. I really enjoyed that. / But, do you think it's too topical? Damn, I wish this event were tonight.
jokes.setup: Liz praises Jack's estate tax joke. Jack then worries it's too topical.
jokes.punchline: 'Damn, I wish this event were tonight' — Jack realizes topicality is time-sensitive and is upset the joke can't be deployed immediately.
jokes.explanation: A moderate joke. Jack's concern about joke shelf-life is a comedian's concern, which is slightly meta — the powerful executive thinking like a stand-up comedian. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: It's after 6:00. What am I, a farmer?
jokes.setup: Liz asks why Jack is wearing a tux.
jokes.punchline: 'It's after 6:00. What am I, a farmer?' — Jack's explanation treats formal attire after 6pm as an absolute rule, and frames not wearing it as something only farmers (the most unfashionable, practical-dress class) would do.
jokes.explanation: The co-equal best joke in the episode alongside 'medicine's not a science.' 'It's after 6:00. What am I, a farmer?' is a perfect joke: eight words, complete character encapsulation, logical structure (after 6pm = tuxedo, non-tuxedo = farmer), and a genuine cultural touchstone for the series. The farmer inversion — using the most rural, working-class archetype as the standard against which Jack measures himself — is brilliant. Only Jack Donaghy exists in a world where 'farmer' is the operative insult. This is the kind of joke that defines a character forever. Quotability is 10 — this is one of the most-quoted lines in the show's run.

jokes.text: The chaos at the Conan taping: Kenneth trying to navigate the studio, pages coming through, Conan's announcer beginning Tracy's introduction.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has the pills but needs to get them to Tracy before he goes on.
jokes.punchline: The comedic escalation of the chase — pager interruptions, crew members blocking, the countdown — builds to a slapstick physical comedy sequence.
jokes.explanation: A structural comedy set piece more than a joke. The escalation works as entertainment but there's no specific joke to isolate — it's cumulative chaos comedy. Functional but not exceptional in writing terms.

jokes.text: Mr. Blue man. You're gonna tell me my feet stink? You don't even have feet. Blue man! / Blue man, where your feet at?
jokes.setup: Tracy has a final confrontation with the Blue Man before going on stage.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's argument — 'you don't even have feet' as a counter to the Blue Man's apparent foot comment — creates an absurdist debate about foot odor where Tracy holds the logical high ground against a hallucination.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the Blue Man gag — the specific accusation of foot odor and Tracy's logical counter ('you don't even have feet') creates a surreal debate with absurdist internal consistency. 'Blue man, where your feet at?' as a challenge is a funny line.

jokes.text: Conan introduces Tracy as being known for 'President Homeboy' and 'Honky Grandma Be Tripping,' and notes 'you may know him from his last appearance on this show, when he tried to stab me in the face.'
jokes.setup: Conan introduces Tracy Jordan for his appearance.
jokes.punchline: The fake movie titles ('Honky Grandma Be Tripping') are great, but the real punchline is Conan's clinical reference to Tracy trying to stab him in the face — listed alongside his credits as a neutral biographical fact.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback with strong execution. 'Honky Grandma Be Tripping' is a perfectly calibrated fake-Tracy-movie title. But listing 'tried to stab me in the face' as a credential alongside film titles — in the same neutral announcer tone — is the real joke. Strong character integration for Conan-as-character.

jokes.text: Tracy appears on stage, immediately takes off his pants, and has to be physically wrestled into a chair while Liz and the crew shout 'Pants on. Pants on. Sit in the chair, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Tracy walks out for his Conan appearance after receiving partial medication.
jokes.punchline: The de-pantsing and chair struggle — narrated through desperate commands from the sideline — is the physical culmination of the episode's entire Tracy arc.
jokes.explanation: Strong physical comedy set piece. The escalating commands ('Pants on. Pants on. Sit in the chair, buddy. Sit. Oh!') are performed as a comedic litany. High impact despite moderate craft score — physical comedy lands harder in-room.

jokes.text: Conan: 'That was great, and you're— And he's asleep. Which...is okay, 'cause at least he didn't murder me.'
jokes.setup: Tracy finally sits in the chair and immediately passes out from the medication.
jokes.punchline: Conan's bar for success: Tracy being unconscious is acceptable because 'at least he didn't murder me.' The lowered expectations are the joke.
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode button joke. The entire Tracy arc resolves in Conan's lowered expectations: passing out = success. 'At least he didn't murder me' is extremely quotable and a perfect callback to the stabbing robot premise. The structure — building the entire episode to 'he's asleep' as a win — is excellent.

jokes.text: Jack takes back the prescription bottle from Liz with 'Hey, you did good, kid. Give me that.' — and apparently pockets the pills.
jokes.setup: The Conan crisis is resolved; Liz hands Jack something.
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'Give me that' implies he's keeping the prescription drugs — a darkly funny character beat implying Jack has personal use for whatever Dr. Spaceman prescribed.
jokes.explanation: A nicely dark character beat. The implication that Jack casually confiscates medication is funny and slightly alarming in equal measure — consistent with his approach to power.

jokes.text: Dennis has ordered Liz a cheeseburger — she's overjoyed: 'Oh, Dennis. Thank you. Thank you, thank you. Thank you so much.'
jokes.setup: Liz comes home exhausted. She'd been set up to break up with Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's one act of thoughtfulness — an unasked-for cheeseburger — completely resets Liz's plans to dump him. Her effusive gratitude reveals how low the bar is.
jokes.explanation: A strong emotional comedy beat and the episode's Liz arc payoff. The cheeseburger is the perfect callback to Liz's low standards — it's not a grand gesture, it's the minimum, and she's ecstatic. The 'thank you, thank you, thank you so much' escalation is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: So what did you want to talk to me about, huh? / Nothing. I forget. / I just want to listen to you play Halo 'til I fall asleep.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks what Liz wanted to talk about (the breakup).
jokes.punchline: 'I just want to listen to you play Halo 'til I fall asleep' — Liz has completely abandoned the breakup plan. Her 'happy ending' is falling asleep to video game sounds, which is darkly funny commentary on her romantic standards.
jokes.explanation: A strong character button. 'Listen to you play Halo 'til I fall asleep' as Liz's romantic ideal is a devastating portrait of settling — which is exactly what the doctor (joke #6) suggested she should do. This is structural payoff for the doctor's 'maybe it's time to settle' advice. Liz has settled, and it's because she got a cheeseburger.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Ah, that's baloney! How did the grenade not kill him? He was standing right next to it. You know what, Liz? This controller's defective.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is playing Halo while Liz has already fallen asleep.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's complete self-absorption — blaming the controller for his failure, totally unaware Liz is asleep — is the perfect coda to his characterization.
jokes.explanation: A solid character button. The controller-blaming is quintessential Dennis — he can't accept personal responsibility even in Halo. The visual of Liz asleep while he rants is the real joke.

jokes.text: Kenneth's final talking-head/interview: reveals he got started in the NBC page program and is now 'making hit movies with my good friend and roommate, Zach Braff.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth appears to be in a confessional or interview giving his life story.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's completely implausible claim that he makes hit movies with Zach Braff — delivered with complete sincerity — is a perfect absurdist Kenneth joke.
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist tag. Kenneth being Zach Braff's roommate and hit-movie collaborator is an impossibly specific and hilarious fabrication — or perhaps sincere delusion. The 'good friend and roommate' specificity is the key. Kenneth's talking-head sincerity makes it land.

jokes.text: Interviewer/Conan: 'What? / Who told you that?' — Kenneth has apparently also claimed other untrue things; the interviewer is confounded.
jokes.setup: Kenneth continues his confessional/interview with Conan.
jokes.punchline: Conan's 'Who told you that?' implies Kenneth has been stating false facts as established truths, and this is at least the second such claim.
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat. Conan's 'Who told you that?' suggests Kenneth's worldview is built on misinformation, which is both funny and slightly dark. Works better on rewatch when you understand Kenneth's character fully.

jokes.text: Kenneth reveals he knows how to clog dance. Conan doesn't believe anyone wants to see this. Kenneth does it anyway. Conan: 'You're a weird guy, Kenneth.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth mentions an unexpected skill — clog dancing.
jokes.punchline: Despite Conan's genuine doubt, Kenneth demonstrates clog dancing and earns surprised appreciation — 'You're a weird guy, Kenneth' delivered with warmth.
jokes.explanation: A sweet, funny episode coda. Kenneth clog-dancing for Conan O'Brien is a perfectly absurd image. 'You're a weird guy, Kenneth' delivered warmly by Conan is a good character-affirming button. The physical comedy of the actual clogging would land well on screen.

jokes.text: Well, yes. I do know how to clog. But I don't think anybody wants to see me do that. / You do? Really? Okay.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is still being interviewed. He mentions knowing how to clog dance.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's self-effacing 'I don't think anybody wants to see that' is immediately challenged, and he accepts the invitation — Kenneth clog dancing on late night television is the final escalation of his inexplicable hidden talents.
jokes.explanation: A good Kenneth comedy beat. His hidden rural skill (clogging) being requested on late-night TV is consistent with the show's treatment of Kenneth as a mysterious figure from another era. The visual of him clogging on the Conan stage is implied and funny.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'See you tomorrow, Mr. O'Brien.' — ending with Kenneth's formal address even after this intimate weird bonding moment.
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Conan have just had a bizarre moment of connection.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth reverts to 'Mr. O'Brien' — maintaining absolute formality after dancing for a celebrity — which is perfect Kenneth.
jokes.explanation: A small but perfectly observed character button. Kenneth's formal address underlines his consistent deference even in vulnerable moments. Economy is the strength.

tmdb_overview: Jack bumps Jenna's scheduled appearance on 'Late Night with Conan O'Brien' by booking new star Tracy. Jenna, still irate over watching the show change to "TGS with Tracy Jordan," lashes out at Liz. To make matters worse, Tracy's gone off his medication and he's about to go on national television.
insight: Tracy's chaos sustains 65 jokes across 22 minutes without losing comedic momentum.
